Module 1. Language, sets, logic and numbers

Notes for module 1, with explanations, examples and exercises.

1.1 Elements of set theory and logic

Definition 1.1 Membership in the module

x∈Ax \in Ax∈A is read "xxx belongs to AAA": xxx is an element of AAA. x∉Ax \notin Ax∈/A is read "xxx does not belong to AAA". The symbols ∈\in∈ and ∉\notin∈/ are used only between an element (on the left) and a set (on the right).

Definition 1.2 Inclusion in the module

A⊆BA \subseteq BA⊆B is read "AAA is contained (or included) in BBB" or "AAA is a subset of BBB": every element of AAA is also an element of BBB. This does not rule out A=BA = BA=B. A⊂BA \subset BA⊂B (or A⊊BA \subsetneq BA⊊B) means that A⊆BA \subseteq BA⊆B and, in addition, A≠BA \ne BA=B: AAA is strictly included in BBB. A⊈BA \not\subseteq BA⊆B means that at least one element of AAA is not in BBB.

Rule 1.1 When two sets are equal in the module

A=BA = BA=B if and only if A⊆BA \subseteq BA⊆B and B⊆AB \subseteq AB⊆A: they have exactly the same elements.

Definition 1.3 Power set in the module

The power set (insieme delle parti) of XXX, denoted by P(X)\mathcal{P}(X)P(X), is the set whose elements are all the subsets of XXX, including ∅\varnothing∅ and XXX:

P(X)={A∣A⊆X}\mathcal{P}(X) = \{A \mid A \subseteq X\}P(X)={A∣A⊆X}
Rule 1.2 How many subsets there are in the module

If XXX has nnn elements, P(X)\mathcal{P}(X)P(X) has 2n2^n2n elements. The reason: to build a subset you decide, element by element, "I take it" or "I leave it out". That is nnn choices with 2 options each: 2⋅2⋯2=2n2 \cdot 2 \cdots 2 = 2^n2⋅2⋯2=2n. The case n=0n = 0n=0 works too: P(∅)={∅}\mathcal{P}(\varnothing) = \{\varnothing\}P(∅)={∅} has 20=12^0 = 120=1 element.

Definition 1.4 The operations in the module
  • Intersection: A∩B={x∣x∈A and x∈B}A \cap B = \{x \mid x \in A \text{ and } x \in B\}A∩B={x∣x∈A and x∈B}, the elements in common. If A∩B=∅A \cap B = \varnothingA∩B=∅, AAA and BBB are called disjoint.
  • Union: A∪B={x∣x∈A or x∈B}A \cup B = \{x \mid x \in A \text{ or } x \in B\}A∪B={x∣x∈A or x∈B}, the elements that are in at least one of the two (possibly in both).
  • Difference: A∖B={x∣x∈A and x∉B}A \setminus B = \{x \mid x \in A \text{ and } x \notin B\}A∖B={x∣x∈A and x∈/B}, the elements of AAA that are not in BBB (also written A−BA - BA−B).
  • Symmetric difference: A Δ BA \,\Delta\, BAΔB, the elements that are in only one of the two sets: A Δ B=(A∖B)∪(B∖A)A \,\Delta\, B = (A \setminus B) \cup (B \setminus A)AΔB=(A∖B)∪(B∖A).
  • Complement of AAA in XXX: A‾=X∖A={x∈X∣x∉A}\overline{A} = X \setminus A = \{x \in X \mid x \notin A\}A=X∖A={x∈X∣x∈/A}.
  • Cartesian product: A×B={(a,b)∣a∈A, b∈B}A \times B = \{(a, b) \mid a \in A,\ b \in B\}A×B={(a,b)∣a∈A, b∈B}, the set of ordered pairs with the first element in AAA and the second in BBB.
Rule 1.3 Useful properties in the module
  • A∩B⊆A⊆A∪BA \cap B \subseteq A \subseteq A \cup BA∩B⊆A⊆A∪B.
  • If A⊆BA \subseteq BA⊆B, then A∩B=AA \cap B = AA∩B=A and A∪B=BA \cup B = BA∪B=B.
  • De Morgan's laws: A∪B‾=A‾∩B‾\overline{A \cup B} = \overline{A} \cap \overline{B}A∪B=A∩B and A∩B‾=A‾∪B‾\overline{A \cap B} = \overline{A} \cup \overline{B}A∩B=A∪B.
  • To count, write ∣A∣|A|∣A∣ for the number of elements of AAA: then ∣A∪B∣=∣A∣+∣B∣−∣A∩B∣|A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B|∣A∪B∣=∣A∣+∣B∣−∣A∩B∣ (otherwise you would count the common elements twice) and ∣A×B∣=∣A∣⋅∣B∣|A \times B| = |A| \cdot |B|∣A×B∣=∣A∣⋅∣B∣.
Definition 1.5 Logical statement in the module

A statement (or proposition) is a sentence that can be objectively established as true or false. Every statement is either true or false, never both: its truth value is T (true; in Italian V, vero) or F (false; falso).

Definition 1.6 Predicate in the module

A predicate is a sentence that contains one or more variables: it becomes true or false only when you give the variables a value. Example: P(x)P(x)P(x): "x2>4x^2 > 4x2>4", with x∈Zx \in \Zx∈Z. P(3)P(3)P(3) is true, P(1)P(1)P(1) is false.

Definition 1.7 Quantifiers in the module
  • ∀\forall∀ is the universal quantifier, read "for every" (or "for all").
  • ∃\exists∃ is the existential quantifier, read "there exists" (at least one).
  • ∃!\exists!∃! is read "there exists one and only one".
Definition 1.8 The connectives in the module
  • Negation ¬p\lnot p¬p ("not ppp"): true when ppp is false, false when ppp is true.
  • Conjunction p∧qp \wedge qp∧q ("ppp and qqq"): true only if ppp and qqq are both true.
  • Inclusive disjunction p∨qp \vee qp∨q ("ppp or qqq"): false only if ppp and qqq are both false.
  • Exclusive disjunction p ∨˙ qp \,\dot{\vee}\, qp∨˙q ("either ppp or qqq"): true if exactly one of the two is true.
  • Implication p⇒qp \Rightarrow qp⇒q ("if ppp then qqq"): false only if ppp is true and qqq is false. ppp is called the antecedent (or hypothesis), qqq the consequent (or conclusion).
  • Biconditional (double implication, or logical equivalence) p⇔qp \Leftrightarrow qp⇔q ("ppp if and only if qqq"): true if ppp and qqq have the same truth value. It means p⇒qp \Rightarrow qp⇒q and also q⇒pq \Rightarrow pq⇒p.

Rule 1.4 Necessary and sufficient condition in the module

If p⇒qp \Rightarrow qp⇒q is true:

  • ppp is a sufficient condition for qqq: ppp holding is enough for qqq to hold;
  • qqq is a necessary condition for ppp: without qqq there cannot be ppp.

If p⇔qp \Leftrightarrow qp⇔q holds, each one is a necessary and sufficient condition for the other.

Rule 1.5 The implications related to p⇒qp \Rightarrow qp⇒q in the module

Example: "if a number is a multiple of 4, then it is even" is true; the contrapositive "if a number is not even, then it is not a multiple of 4" is true as well; the converse "if a number is even, then it is a multiple of 4" is false (counterexample: 6).

Definition 1.9 Counterexample in the module

To show that a statement of the form "for every xxx, P(x)P(x)P(x) holds", or "if HHH then TTT", is false, a counterexample is enough: a single case that satisfies the hypotheses but not the conclusion.

1.2 Numbers

Definition 1.10 Natural numbers in the module

N={0,1,2,3,… }\N = \{0, 1, 2, 3, \dots\}N={0,1,2,3,…} is the set of natural numbers. It has infinitely many elements and the smallest is 000.

Rule 1.8 Properties of addition and multiplication in the module

For every aaa, bbb, ccc:

propertyadditionmultiplication
commutativea+b=b+aa + b = b + aa+b=b+aa⋅b=b⋅aa \cdot b = b \cdot aa⋅b=b⋅a
associative(a+b)+c=a+(b+c)(a + b) + c = a + (b + c)(a+b)+c=a+(b+c)(a⋅b)⋅c=a⋅(b⋅c)(a \cdot b) \cdot c = a \cdot (b \cdot c)(a⋅b)⋅c=a⋅(b⋅c)
identity elementa+0=0+a=aa + 0 = 0 + a = aa+0=0+a=aa⋅1=1⋅a=aa \cdot 1 = 1 \cdot a = aa⋅1=1⋅a=a

The distributive property links the two operations: a(b+c)=ab+aca(b + c) = ab + aca(b+c)=ab+ac.

Definition 1.11 Divisors and prime numbers in the module

aaa is divisible by bbb (bbb is a divisor of aaa, aaa is a multiple of bbb) if a=b⋅ka = b \cdot ka=b⋅k with kkk an integer. A natural number p>1p > 1p>1 is prime if its only positive divisors are 111 and ppp: 2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23,…2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, \dots2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23,… The number 111 is not prime and 222 is the only even prime.

Rule 1.9 Prime factorisation, gcd and lcm in the module

Every natural number greater than 1 can be written in only one way as a product of prime numbers (up to the order of the factors). Example: 360=23⋅32⋅5360 = 2^3 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5360=23⋅32⋅5.

  • gcd (greatest common divisor; in Italian MCD, massimo comune divisore): the product of the common prime factors, each with the smallest exponent.
  • lcm (least common multiple; in Italian mcm, minimo comune multiplo): the product of the prime factors, common and non-common, each with the largest exponent.
  • For two numbers, gcd(a,b)⋅lcm(a,b)=a⋅b\text{gcd}(a, b) \cdot \text{lcm}(a, b) = a \cdot bgcd(a,b)⋅lcm(a,b)=a⋅b.
Definition 1.12 Integers in the module

Z={…,−3,−2,−1,0,1,2,3,… }\Z = \{\dots, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots\}Z={…,−3,−2,−1,0,1,2,3,…}: the natural numbers together with their opposites. The opposite (additive inverse) of aaa is the number −a-a−a such that a+(−a)=0a + (-a) = 0a+(−a)=0: the opposite of 444 is −4-4−4, the opposite of −7-7−7 is 777, the opposite of 000 is 000.

Rule 1.10 Sign rule and brackets in the module

In products and quotients: equal signs give +++, different signs give −-−. So (−3)⋅(−4)=12(-3) \cdot (-4) = 12(−3)⋅(−4)=12, (−3)⋅4=−12(-3) \cdot 4 = -12(−3)⋅4=−12, (−12):(−4)=3(-12) : (-4) = 3(−12):(−4)=3. A bracket preceded by −-− is removed by changing the sign of all the terms inside: 5−(3−x)=5−3+x=2+x5 - (3 - x) = 5 - 3 + x = 2 + x5−(3−x)=5−3+x=2+x.

Definition 1.13 Rational numbers in the module

Q={mn∣m,n∈Z, n≠0}\Q = \left\{ \dfrac{m}{n} \mid m, n \in \Z,\ n \ne 0 \right\}Q={nm​∣m,n∈Z, n=0} is the set of rational numbers: those that can be written as a fraction of two integers, with a non-zero denominator.

Rule 1.11 Operations with fractions in the module
ab+cd=ad+bcbdab⋅cd=acbdab:cd=ab⋅dc(ab)n=anbn\frac{a}{b} + \frac{c}{d} = \frac{ad + bc}{bd} \qquad \frac{a}{b} \cdot \frac{c}{d} = \frac{ac}{bd} \qquad \frac{a}{b} : \frac{c}{d} = \frac{a}{b} \cdot \frac{d}{c} \qquad \left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^n = \frac{a^n}{b^n}ba​+dc​=bdad+bc​ba​⋅dc​=bdac​ba​:dc​=ba​⋅cd​(ba​)n=bnan​

When adding, it is best to use the lcm of the denominators as the denominator. To compare two fractions with positive denominators: ab<cd\tfrac{a}{b} < \tfrac{c}{d}ba​<dc​ if and only if ad<bcad < bcad<bc.

Rule 1.12 Terminating or repeating? in the module

Reduce the fraction to lowest terms and factorise the denominator: if it contains only the prime factors 222 and 555, the decimal is terminating; if another prime appears as well, it is repeating.

  • 740\tfrac{7}{40}407​: 40=23⋅540 = 2^3 \cdot 540=23⋅5, terminating (0.1750.1750.175).
  • 730\tfrac{7}{30}307​: 30=2⋅3⋅530 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 530=2⋅3⋅5 contains 3, repeating (0.23‾0.2\overline{3}0.23).
  • 912\tfrac{9}{12}129​: first reduce it, 912=34\tfrac{9}{12} = \tfrac34129​=43​, and 4=224 = 2^24=22 gives a terminating decimal (0.750.750.75).
Definition 1.14 Percentage in the module

"ppp per cent", written p%p\%p%, means p100\tfrac{p}{100}100p​. p%p\%p% of a quantity xxx is p100⋅x\tfrac{p}{100} \cdot x100p​⋅x: 15% of 80 is 0.15⋅80=120.15 \cdot 80 = 120.15⋅80=12.

Rule 1.13 Increases and discounts are multiplications in the module
  • Increasing xxx by p%p\%p%: x⋅(1+p100)x \cdot \left(1 + \tfrac{p}{100}\right)x⋅(1+100p​). A 20% increase is ×1.2\times 1.2×1.2.
  • Decreasing xxx by p%p\%p%: x⋅(1−p100)x \cdot \left(1 - \tfrac{p}{100}\right)x⋅(1−100p​). A 5% discount is ×0.95\times 0.95×0.95.
  • Two changes in a row are multiplied, not added.
  • To go back to the initial value, you divide by the same factor.

Rule 1.15 The sign of a power in the module

A negative base with an even exponent gives a positive result, with an odd exponent a negative one: (−2)4=16(-2)^4 = 16(−2)4=16, (−2)3=−8(-2)^3 = -8(−2)3=−8. Watch the brackets: −24=−(24)=−16-2^4 = -(2^4) = -16−24=−(24)=−16, whereas (−2)4=16(-2)^4 = 16(−2)4=16.

Definition 1.16 Square root and nnnth root in the module

For a≥0a \ge 0a≥0, a\sqrt{a}a​ is the number greater than or equal to zero whose square is aaa: 25=5\sqrt{25} = 525​=5, not ±5\pm 5±5 ("plus or minus 5"), even though (−5)2=25(-5)^2 = 25(−5)2=25 as well. More generally, an\sqrt[n]{a}na​ is the number which, raised to the power nnn, gives aaa. With an even index nnn you need a≥0a \ge 0a≥0 and the result is ≥0\ge 0≥0; with an odd index any aaa is fine: −83=−2\sqrt[3]{-8} = -23−8​=−2. Roots can also be written as powers with a fractional exponent: amn=am/n\sqrt[n]{a^m} = a^{m/n}nam​=am/n (for a>0a > 0a>0). For example 82/3=(83)2=22=48^{2/3} = \left(\sqrt[3]{8}\right)^2 = 2^2 = 482/3=(38​)2=22=4.

The last one holds for every real aaa: (−3)2=9=3=∣−3∣\sqrt{(-3)^2} = \sqrt9 = 3 = |-3|(−3)2​=9​=3=∣−3∣.

Definition 1.17 Irrational numbers in the module

An irrational number is a real number that cannot be written as a fraction of integers. Its decimal expansion is infinite and non-repeating: 2=1.41421356…\sqrt2 = 1.41421356\ldots2​=1.41421356…, π=3.14159265…\pi = 3.14159265\ldotsπ=3.14159265…, e=2.71828…e = 2.71828\ldotse=2.71828… (Euler's number, also called Napier's constant).

Rule 1.17 When a root is rational in the module

If nnn is a natural number, n\sqrt{n}n​ is rational only when nnn is a perfect square (49=7\sqrt{49} = 749​=7); otherwise it is irrational: 3\sqrt33​, 5\sqrt55​, 8\sqrt88​, 12\sqrt{12}12​ are irrational. For a positive rational qqq: q\sqrt{q}q​ is rational if and only if qqq is the square of a rational number. For example 925=35\sqrt{\tfrac{9}{25}} = \tfrac35259​​=53​.

Rule 1.18 Operations between rational and irrational numbers in the module
  • rational +++ irrational is irrational: 1+21 + \sqrt21+2​;
  • non-zero rational ×\times× irrational is irrational: 323\sqrt232​;
  • the sum and the product of two irrational numbers can be rational: 2+(−2)=0\sqrt2 + \left(-\sqrt2\right) = 02​+(−2​)=0 and 2⋅8=16=4\sqrt2 \cdot \sqrt8 = \sqrt{16} = 42​⋅8​=16​=4.
Definition 1.18 Real numbers in the module

R\RR is the set of real numbers: the union of the rational and the irrational numbers. The real numbers correspond to the points of a line: once an origin (the point 000), a direction and a unit of length have been fixed, each point corresponds to one and only one real number and vice versa. This is the real line.

Rule 1.19 Between two numbers there is always another one in the module

Between two different rational numbers there is always another rational number, for example their mean: between 13\tfrac1331​ and 12\tfrac1221​ there is 12(13+12)=512\tfrac12\left(\tfrac13 + \tfrac12\right) = \tfrac{5}{12}21​(31​+21​)=125​. Repeating the argument, you find infinitely many. With decimals it is even quicker: between 2.712.712.71 and 2.722.722.72 there are 2.7112.7112.711, 2.7152.7152.715, 2.71992.71992.7199 and infinitely many others.

Definition 1.19 Intervals in the module

An interval is the set of real numbers between two endpoints a<ba < ba<b (a segment of the line) or the set of real numbers greater than or less than a given number (a half-line). A square bracket means the endpoint is included, a round bracket means it is excluded. Half-lines involve the symbols +∞+\infty+∞ ("plus infinity") and −∞-\infty−∞ ("minus infinity").

Module 2. Polynomials and factorisation

Notes for module 2, with explanations, examples and exercises.

2.1 Polynomials and factorisation

Definition 2.1 Monomial in the module

A monomial is the product of a number, the coefficient, and one or more letters with natural-number exponents, the literal part. Examples: −5x3-5x^3−5x3, 23x2y\tfrac23 x^2 y32​x2y, 777 (a number on its own is a monomial with no letters). The degree of a monomial is the sum of the exponents of its letters: −5x3-5x^3−5x3 has degree 3, 23x2y\tfrac23 x^2 y32​x2y has degree 2+1=32 + 1 = 32+1=3, 777 has degree 0. Two monomials are like (similar) if they have the same literal part: 4x24x^24x2 and −x2-x^2−x2 are like monomials, 4x24x^24x2 and 4x34x^34x3 are not.

Rule 2.1 Operations with monomials in the module
  • You can add only like monomials, by adding the coefficients: 4x2−x2=3x24x^2 - x^2 = 3x^24x2−x2=3x2. On the other hand, 4x2+4x34x^2 + 4x^34x2+4x3 stays as it is.
  • In a product you multiply the coefficients and add the exponents of the same letters: (3x2)(−2x5)=−6x7(3x^2)(-2x^5) = -6x^7(3x2)(−2x5)=−6x7.
  • In a power you raise the coefficient to the power and multiply the exponents: (−2x3)2=4x6(-2x^3)^2 = 4x^6(−2x3)2=4x6.
  • In a division you divide the coefficients and subtract the exponents: 12x5:4x2=3x312x^5 : 4x^2 = 3x^312x5:4x2=3x3.
Definition 2.2 Polynomial in one variable in the module

A polynomial in the variable xxx is an expression of the form

P(x)=anxn+an−1xn−1+⋯+a2x2+a1x+a0n∈NP(x) = a_n x^n + a_{n-1} x^{n-1} + \dots + a_2 x^2 + a_1 x + a_0 \qquad n \in \NP(x)=an​xn+an−1​xn−1+⋯+a2​x2+a1​x+a0​n∈N
  • an,an−1,…,a0a_n, a_{n-1}, \dots, a_0an​,an−1​,…,a0​ are the coefficients: numbers taken from a number set (Z\ZZ, Q\QQ or R\RR).
  • If an≠0a_n \ne 0an​=0, nnn is the degree of the polynomial and ana_nan​ is the leading coefficient (the coefficient of the highest-degree term).
  • a0a_0a0​ is the constant term.
Rule 2.2 Identity principle for polynomials in the module

Two polynomials are equal, that is, they give the same value for every xxx, if and only if they have the same coefficients, term by term.

Rule 2.3 The special products in the module

Rule 2.4 Division with remainder in the module

Given A(x)A(x)A(x) (the dividend) and B(x)B(x)B(x) (the divisor, non-zero), there exist two unique polynomials Q(x)Q(x)Q(x), the quotient, and R(x)R(x)R(x), the remainder, such that

A(x)=B(x)⋅Q(x)+R(x)with degree of R<degree of BA(x) = B(x) \cdot Q(x) + R(x) \qquad \text{with degree of } R < \text{degree of } BA(x)=B(x)⋅Q(x)+R(x)with degree of R<degree of B

If R(x)=0R(x) = 0R(x)=0, AAA is said to be divisible by BBB, and BBB is a factor of AAA.

Rule 2.5 Remainder theorem in the module

The remainder of the division of P(x)P(x)P(x) by x−ax - ax−a is P(a)P(a)P(a).

Rule 2.6 Factor theorem (Ruffini's theorem) in the module

P(x)P(x)P(x) is divisible by x−ax - ax−a if and only if P(a)=0P(a) = 0P(a)=0. A number aaa such that P(a)=0P(a) = 0P(a)=0 is called a root (or zero) of the polynomial.

Rule 2.7 Trinomial x2+Sx+Px^2 + Sx + Px2+Sx+P in the module

If you find two numbers mmm and nnn with sum m+n=Sm + n = Sm+n=S and product m⋅n=Pm \cdot n = Pm⋅n=P, then

x2+Sx+P=(x+m)(x+n)x^2 + Sx + P = (x + m)(x + n)x2+Sx+P=(x+m)(x+n)

Indeed, (x+m)(x+n)=x2+(m+n)x+mn(x + m)(x + n) = x^2 + (m + n)x + mn(x+m)(x+n)=x2+(m+n)x+mn.

Rule 2.8 Where to look for rational roots in the module

If P(x)P(x)P(x) has integer coefficients and the reduced fraction pq\tfrac{p}{q}qp​ is one of its roots, then ppp divides the constant term and qqq divides the leading coefficient. In practice the candidates are

±divisors of the constant termdivisors of the leading coefficient\pm \frac{\text{divisors of the constant term}}{\text{divisors of the leading coefficient}}±divisors of the leading coefficientdivisors of the constant term​

If the leading coefficient is 111, the candidates are just the divisors of the constant term, with the +++ sign and with the −-− sign.

Rule 2.9 Factorised form and roots in the module

A polynomial of degree nnn has at most nnn real roots; it can have fewer, or none. If it has exactly nnn, namely x1,x2,…,xnx_1, x_2, \dots, x_nx1​,x2​,…,xn​ (a root that appears twice, as in (x−5)2(x - 5)^2(x−5)2, is counted twice), then

P(x)=an(x−x1)(x−x2)⋯(x−xn)P(x) = a_n (x - x_1)(x - x_2) \cdots (x - x_n)P(x)=an​(x−x1​)(x−x2​)⋯(x−xn​)

where ana_nan​ is the leading coefficient. For example 2x3−3x2−3x+22x^3 - 3x^2 - 3x + 22x3−3x2−3x+2 has leading coefficient 222 and roots −1-1−1, 222 and 12\tfrac1221​, so it is equal to 2(x+1)(x−2)(x−12)=(x+1)(x−2)(2x−1)2(x + 1)(x - 2)\left(x - \tfrac12\right) = (x + 1)(x - 2)(2x - 1)2(x+1)(x−2)(x−21​)=(x+1)(x−2)(2x−1).

Rule 2.10 When a polynomial cannot be factorised in the module
  • Every first-degree polynomial is irreducible.
  • A second-degree polynomial factorises into two first-degree factors (with real coefficients) if and only if it has real roots. x2+1x^2 + 1x2+1, x2+4x^2 + 4x2+4 and x2+x+1x^2 + x + 1x2+x+1 have none: they are irreducible.
  • In module 3 you will use the discriminant b2−4acb^2 - 4acb2−4ac: if it is negative, the trinomial ax2+bx+cax^2 + bx + cax2+bx+c is irreducible.
Definition 2.3 Algebraic fraction and domain conditions in the module

An algebraic fraction is a quotient A(x)B(x)\dfrac{A(x)}{B(x)}B(x)A(x)​ of two polynomials. It makes sense only where the denominator is not zero: the domain conditions (C.E., from the Italian condizioni di esistenza) are B(x)≠0B(x) \ne 0B(x)=0. Example: x+5x2−9\dfrac{x + 5}{x^2 - 9}x2−9x+5​ exists for x2−9≠0x^2 - 9 \ne 0x2−9=0, that is, for x≠3x \ne 3x=3 and x≠−3x \ne -3x=−3.

Module 3. First- and second-degree equations and inequalities, systems

Notes for module 3, with explanations, examples and exercises.

3.1 First-degree equations and inequalities

Definition 3.1 Equation and solution in the module

An equation is an equality between two expressions that contains a letter, the unknown (usually xxx). The expression to the left of the equals sign is the left-hand side (primo membro), the one to the right is the right-hand side (secondo membro). A solution is a number that, put in place of xxx, makes the equality true. Solving an equation means finding all its solutions.

Rule 3.1 The two equivalence principles in the module
  1. First principle. If you add or subtract the same expression on both sides, you get an equivalent equation.
  2. Second principle. If you multiply or divide both sides by the same non-zero number, you get an equivalent equation.
Rule 3.2 Equivalence principles for inequalities in the module
  1. Adding or subtracting the same expression on both sides does not change the solutions (transposition works as in equations).
  2. Multiplying or dividing both sides by a positive number does not change the solutions.
  3. Multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number changes the direction (verso): <<< becomes >>>, ≤\leq≤ becomes ≥\geq≥ and vice versa.

3.2 Second-degree equations and inequalities

Definition 3.2 Second-degree equation in the module

A second-degree (quadratic) equation in standard form (forma normale) is

ax2+bx+c=0with a≠0ax^2 + bx + c = 0 \qquad \text{with } a \neq 0ax2+bx+c=0with a=0

The numbers aaa, bbb, ccc are the coefficients; ccc is called the constant term. The solutions are also called roots and there are at most two of them, denoted by x1x_1x1​ and x2x_2x2​.

Rule 3.3 Zero product property (legge di annullamento del prodotto) in the module

A product equals zero if and only if at least one of the factors equals zero: A⋅B=0A \cdot B = 0A⋅B=0 is equivalent to A=0A = 0A=0 or B=0B = 0B=0.

Rule 3.4 Quadratic formula (formula risolutiva) in the module

The solutions of ax2+bx+c=0ax^2 + bx + c = 0ax2+bx+c=0 are

x1,2=−b±b2−4ac2ax_{1,2} = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}x1,2​=2a−b±b2−4ac​​

The number under the root is called the discriminant and is denoted by the Greek letter Δ\DeltaΔ ("delta"): Δ=b2−4ac\Delta = b^2 - 4acΔ=b2−4ac.

  • Δ>0\Delta > 0Δ>0: two distinct real solutions, x1=−b−Δ2ax_1 = \frac{-b - \sqrt{\Delta}}{2a}x1​=2a−b−Δ​​ and x2=−b+Δ2ax_2 = \frac{-b + \sqrt{\Delta}}{2a}x2​=2a−b+Δ​​.
  • Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0: two coincident solutions, that is a single solution (called a double solution): x1=x2=−b2ax_1 = x_2 = -\frac{b}{2a}x1​=x2​=−2ab​.
  • Δ<0\Delta < 0Δ<0: no real solutions (the square root of a negative number is not a real number).
Rule 3.5 Reduced formula (when bbb is even) in the module

If bbb is an even number it is easier to work with half of it, b2\frac{b}{2}2b​:

x1,2=−b2±(b2)2−acax_{1,2} = \frac{-\frac{b}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\frac{b}{2}\right)^2 - ac}}{a}x1,2​=a−2b​±(2b​)2−ac​​

The number under the root, (b2)2−ac\left(\frac{b}{2}\right)^2 - ac(2b​)2−ac, is Δ4\frac{\Delta}{4}4Δ​: it has the same sign as Δ\DeltaΔ and decides the number of solutions in the same way. The calculations involve smaller numbers; the result is identical.

Rule 3.6 Factorising the second-degree trinomial in the module

If Δ≥0\Delta \geq 0Δ≥0 and x1x_1x1​, x2x_2x2​ are the solutions of ax2+bx+c=0ax^2 + bx + c = 0ax2+bx+c=0, then

ax2+bx+c=a(x−x1)(x−x2)ax^2 + bx + c = a(x - x_1)(x - x_2)ax2+bx+c=a(x−x1​)(x−x2​)

If Δ<0\Delta < 0Δ<0 the trinomial cannot be factorised over the real numbers.

Expanding the product you find two very useful relations:

x1+x2=−bax1⋅x2=cax_1 + x_2 = -\frac{b}{a} \qquad\qquad x_1 \cdot x_2 = \frac{c}{a}x1​+x2​=−ab​x1​⋅x2​=ac​

Let x1<x2x_1 < x_2x1​<x2​ be the solutions of the associated equation when Δ>0\Delta > 0Δ>0, and x0=−b2ax_0 = -\frac{b}{2a}x0​=−2ab​ the double solution when Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0.

In short, with Δ>0\Delta > 0Δ>0: direction >>> → outer intervals, direction <<< → inner interval. If a<0a < 0a<0 multiply everything by −1-1−1, reverse the direction and then use the table.

3.3 Systems of equations

Definition 3.3 System and solution in the module

A system is a group of two or more equations that must hold at the same time. It is written with a curly bracket:

{x+y=5x−y=1\begin{cases} x + y = 5 \\ x - y = 1 \end{cases}{x+y=5x−y=1​

A solution of a system in two unknowns is an ordered pair (x,y)(x, y)(x,y) that makes all the equations true; with three unknowns it is a triple (x,y,z)(x, y, z)(x,y,z), and so on. Here the solution is (3,2)(3, 2)(3,2): 3+2=53 + 2 = 53+2=5 and 3−2=13 - 2 = 13−2=1. The pair (2,3)(2, 3)(2,3), on the other hand, does not work, because the order matters.

Definition 3.4 Degree of a system in the module

The degree of a polynomial equation in several unknowns is the highest degree of its terms; in a term such as x2yx^2yx2y you add the exponents (2+1=32 + 1 = 32+1=3). The degree of a system is the product of the degrees of its equations. For example:

{x+y=3xy=2 has degree 1⋅2=2,{x3−y=0x2+y2=1 has degree 3⋅2=6.\begin{cases} x + y = 3 \\ xy = 2 \end{cases} \text{ has degree } 1 \cdot 2 = 2, \qquad \begin{cases} x^3 - y = 0 \\ x^2 + y^2 = 1 \end{cases} \text{ has degree } 3 \cdot 2 = 6.{x+y=3xy=2​ has degree 1⋅2=2,{x3−y=0x2+y2=1​ has degree 3⋅2=6.

For the system a1x+b1y=c1a_1 x + b_1 y = c_1a1​x+b1​y=c1​, a2x+b2y=c2a_2 x + b_2 y = c_2a2​x+b2​y=c2​, with non-zero coefficients:

a1a2=b1b2≠c1c2\frac{a_1}{a_2} = \frac{b_1}{b_2} \neq \frac{c_1}{c_2}a2​a1​​=b2​b1​​=c2​c1​​impossibleparallel and distinct
a1a2=b1b2=c1c2\frac{a_1}{a_2} = \frac{b_1}{b_2} = \frac{c_1}{c_2}a2​a1​​=b2​b1​​=c2​c1​​indeterminatecoincident

Module 4. Rational, radical and absolute value equations and inequalities

Notes for module 4, with explanations, examples and exercises.

4.1 Rational equations and inequalities

Definition 4.1 Rational equations and domain conditions in the module

An equation (or inequality) is rational (fractional, fratta) when the unknown appears in at least one denominator. A fraction makes no sense if its denominator is zero, so first of all you write the domain conditions (C.E. for short, from the Italian condizioni di esistenza): the values of xxx that make a denominator zero must be excluded. The set of allowed values is called the domain (campo di esistenza, or dominio).

Rule 4.1 Rule of signs in the module

A quotient (or a product) is positive if the two factors have the same sign and negative if they have opposite signs:

++=+,−−=+,+−=−,−+=−\frac{+}{+} = +, \qquad \frac{-}{-} = +, \qquad \frac{+}{-} = -, \qquad \frac{-}{+} = -++​=+,−−​=+,−+​=−,+−​=−

A fraction is zero where its numerator is zero and does not exist where its denominator is zero.

4.2 Radical equations and inequalities

Rule 4.2 Even index and odd index in the module
  • Odd index (cube root  3\sqrt[3]{\ }3 ​, fifth root, ...): the root exists for every radicand and has the same sign as the radicand. Examples: 83=2\sqrt[3]{8} = 238​=2, −83=−2\sqrt[3]{-8} = -23−8​=−2.
  • Even index (square root, fourth root, ...): the root exists only if the radicand is greater than or equal to zero, and the result is greater than or equal to zero. Examples: 9=3\sqrt{9} = 39​=3 (not −3-3−3), 164=2\sqrt[4]{16} = 2416​=2, while −4\sqrt{-4}−4​ is not a real number.
Rule 4.3 Raising to a power in the module
  • If nnn is odd, a=ba = ba=b is equivalent to an=bna^n = b^nan=bn for all real numbers aaa and bbb.
  • If nnn is even, a=ba = ba=b is equivalent to an=bna^n = b^nan=bn only if aaa and bbb have the same sign (in Italian, they are concordi). For example −3≠3-3 \neq 3−3=3, but (−3)2=32(-3)^2 = 3^2(−3)2=32.

So when you square an equation, extraneous solutions may appear, which solve the squared equation but not the original one.

Rule 4.4 Square root less than g(x)g(x)g(x) in the module
f(x)<g(x)⟺{f(x)≥0g(x)>0f(x)<g(x)2\sqrt{f(x)} < g(x) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \begin{cases} f(x) \geq 0 \\ g(x) > 0 \\ f(x) < g(x)^2 \end{cases}f(x)​<g(x)⟺⎩⎨⎧​f(x)≥0g(x)>0f(x)<g(x)2​

The double arrow ⟺\Longleftrightarrow⟺ is read "is equivalent to": what is on the left and what is on the right have the same solutions.

  • f(x)≥0f(x) \geq 0f(x)≥0: the root must exist;
  • g(x)>0g(x) > 0g(x)>0: the root is positive or zero, so it can be less than g(x)g(x)g(x) only if g(x)g(x)g(x) is positive;
  • f(x)<g(x)2f(x) < g(x)^2f(x)<g(x)2: now both sides are positive or zero and you can square without changing the direction.

With ≤\leq≤ in place of <<< the system becomes f(x)≥0f(x) \geq 0f(x)≥0, g(x)≥0g(x) \geq 0g(x)≥0, f(x)≤g(x)2f(x) \leq g(x)^2f(x)≤g(x)2.

Rule 4.5 Square root greater than g(x)g(x)g(x) in the module
f(x)>g(x)⟺{g(x)<0f(x)≥0  ∪  {g(x)≥0f(x)>g(x)2\sqrt{f(x)} > g(x) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \begin{cases} g(x) < 0 \\ f(x) \geq 0 \end{cases} \;\cup\; \begin{cases} g(x) \geq 0 \\ f(x) > g(x)^2 \end{cases}f(x)​>g(x)⟺{g(x)<0f(x)≥0​∪{g(x)≥0f(x)>g(x)2​
  • First system: if g(x)g(x)g(x) is negative, the inequality is true wherever the root exists.
  • Second system: if g(x)≥0g(x) \geq 0g(x)≥0 you square; the condition f(x)≥0f(x) \geq 0f(x)≥0 is already contained in f(x)>g(x)2f(x) > g(x)^2f(x)>g(x)2.
  • The solutions are the union of the solutions of the two systems.

With ≥\geq≥ in place of >>>, in the second system you write f(x)≥g(x)2f(x) \geq g(x)^2f(x)≥g(x)2.

4.3 Absolute value equations and inequalities

Definition 4.2 Absolute value (or modulus) in the module

The absolute value (or modulus, modulo) of an expression AAA, written ∣A∣|A|∣A∣, is

∣A∣={Aif A≥0−Aif A<0|A| = \begin{cases} A & \text{if } A \geq 0 \\ -A & \text{if } A < 0 \end{cases}∣A∣={A−A​if A≥0if A<0​

If AAA is positive or zero it leaves it as it is; if AAA is negative it changes its sign. The result is never negative.

Rule 4.6 Useful properties in the module
  • ∣A∣≥0|A| \geq 0∣A∣≥0 always, and ∣A∣=0|A| = 0∣A∣=0 only if A=0A = 0A=0.
  • ∣−A∣=∣A∣|-A| = |A|∣−A∣=∣A∣ and ∣A⋅B∣=∣A∣⋅∣B∣|A \cdot B| = |A| \cdot |B|∣A⋅B∣=∣A∣⋅∣B∣.
  • A2=∣A∣\sqrt{A^2} = |A|A2​=∣A∣: for example (−3)2=9=3\sqrt{(-3)^2} = \sqrt{9} = 3(−3)2​=9​=3.
  • ∣x−a∣|x - a|∣x−a∣ is the distance between the points xxx and aaa on the number line. In particular ∣x∣|x|∣x∣ is the distance of xxx from 000.
Rule 4.7 ∣A(x)∣=c|A(x)| = c∣A(x)∣=c with ccc a number in the module
  • c<0c < 0c<0: no solutions, because an absolute value is never negative.
  • c=0c = 0c=0: it is equivalent to A(x)=0A(x) = 0A(x)=0.
  • c>0c > 0c>0: it is equivalent to A(x)=cA(x) = cA(x)=c or A(x)=−cA(x) = -cA(x)=−c.

The last case comes from the definition. You solve the two systems

{A(x)≥0A(x)=cor{A(x)<0−A(x)=c\begin{cases} A(x) \geq 0 \\ A(x) = c \end{cases} \qquad \text{or} \qquad \begin{cases} A(x) < 0 \\ -A(x) = c \end{cases}{A(x)≥0A(x)=c​or{A(x)<0−A(x)=c​

and take the union of the solutions. With c>0c > 0c>0 the sign conditions are automatically true, and what remains is A(x)=cA(x) = cA(x)=c and A(x)=−cA(x) = -cA(x)=−c.

Rule 4.8 Inequalities with ccc a number in the module

With c>0c > 0c>0:

∣A(x)∣<c  ⟺  −c<A(x)<c∣A(x)∣>c  ⟺  A(x)<−c   or   A(x)>c|A(x)| < c \iff -c < A(x) < c \qquad\qquad |A(x)| > c \iff A(x) < -c \;\text{ or }\; A(x) > c∣A(x)∣<c⟺−c<A(x)<c∣A(x)∣>c⟺A(x)<−c or A(x)>c

With ≤\leq≤ and ≥\geq≥ the endpoints are included. The second case can also be obtained from the definition, by taking the union of the systems A(x)≥0A(x) \geq 0A(x)≥0, A(x)>cA(x) > cA(x)>c and A(x)<0A(x) < 0A(x)<0, −A(x)>c-A(x) > c−A(x)>c.

Thinking of distance: ∣x−a∣<r|x - a| < r∣x−a∣<r gives the points whose distance from aaa is less than rrr, that is the interval (a−r,a+r)(a - r, a + r)(a−r,a+r); ∣x−a∣>r|x - a| > r∣x−a∣>r gives the points farther away than rrr.

Module 5. Analytic geometry: lines and conics

Notes for module 5, with explanations, examples and exercises.

Introduction: the Cartesian plane

Definition 5.1 Cartesian coordinate system in the module

A Cartesian coordinate system is formed by two perpendicular oriented lines that meet at the origin OOO: the axis of abscissas (xxx-axis, horizontal, oriented to the right) and the axis of ordinates (yyy-axis, vertical, oriented upwards). The real numbers are represented on both of them, with 000 at OOO. Every point PPP corresponds to exactly one ordered pair P=(x,y)P = (x, y)P=(x,y): xxx is the xxx-coordinate (abscissa) of PPP, yyy is its yyy-coordinate (ordinate).

Rule 5.1 Distance between two points in the module

The distance between A=(xA,yA)A = (x_A, y_A)A=(xA​,yA​) and B=(xB,yB)B = (x_B, y_B)B=(xB​,yB​) is

d(A,B)=(xB−xA)2+(yB−yA)2d(A, B) = \sqrt{(x_B - x_A)^2 + (y_B - y_A)^2}d(A,B)=(xB​−xA​)2+(yB​−yA​)2​
Rule 5.2 Midpoint in the module

The coordinates of the midpoint of the segment ABABAB are the averages of the coordinates of the endpoints:

M=(xA+xB2,yA+yB2)M = \left(\frac{x_A + x_B}{2}, \frac{y_A + y_B}{2}\right)M=(2xA​+xB​​,2yA​+yB​​)

5.1 The straight line in the Cartesian plane

Definition 5.2 Slope-intercept form in the module

A non-vertical line has equation y=mx+qy = mx + qy=mx+q. The number mmm is the slope (or gradient; in Italian coefficiente angolare or pendenza), the number qqq is the yyy-intercept (ordinata all'origine): the line crosses the yyy-axis at the point (0,q)(0, q)(0,q).

Rule 5.3 All lines, and only lines in the module

Every first-degree equation ax+by+c=0ax + by + c = 0ax+by+c=0, with aaa and bbb not both zero, represents a line; conversely, every line in the plane has an equation of this type, called the general (implicit) form. If b≠0b \ne 0b=0 you can solve for yyy: y=−abx−cby = -\frac{a}{b}x - \frac{c}{b}y=−ba​x−bc​, so

m=−ab,q=−cbm = -\frac{a}{b}, \qquad q = -\frac{c}{b}m=−ba​,q=−bc​
Rule 5.4 Line through a point with a given slope in the module

The line that passes through P=(xP,yP)P = (x_P, y_P)P=(xP​,yP​) and has slope mmm is

y−yP=m(x−xP)y - y_P = m(x - x_P)y−yP​=m(x−xP​)

As mmm varies you get all the lines through PPP except the vertical one, x=xPx = x_Px=xP​.

Rule 5.5 Parallel and perpendicular lines in the module

For r:y=mx+qr: y = mx + qr:y=mx+q and r′:y=m′x+q′r': y = m'x + q'r′:y=m′x+q′:

  • rrr and r′r'r′ are parallel (r∥r′r \parallel r'r∥r′) if and only if m=m′m = m'm=m′;
  • rrr and r′r'r′ are perpendicular (r⊥r′r \perp r'r⊥r′) if and only if m⋅m′=−1m \cdot m' = -1m⋅m′=−1, that is m′=−1mm' = -\frac{1}{m}m′=−m1​: the slope of the perpendicular is the negative reciprocal (antireciproco).

In general form, ax+by+c=0ax + by + c = 0ax+by+c=0 and a′x+b′y+c′=0a'x + b'y + c' = 0a′x+b′y+c′=0 are parallel if ab′=a′bab' = a'bab′=a′b and perpendicular if aa′+bb′=0aa' + bb' = 0aa′+bb′=0. These two conditions also hold for horizontal and vertical lines: two vertical lines are parallel, a horizontal line and a vertical line are perpendicular.

Rule 5.6 Point-to-line distance in the module

The distance of P0=(x0,y0)P_0 = (x_0, y_0)P0​=(x0​,y0​) from the line r:ax+by+c=0r: ax + by + c = 0r:ax+by+c=0 is

d(P0,r)=∣ax0+by0+c∣a2+b2d(P_0, r) = \frac{|ax_0 + by_0 + c|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}d(P0​,r)=a2+b2​∣ax0​+by0​+c∣​

It is the length of the segment P0HP_0HP0​H, where HHH is the foot of the perpendicular drawn from P0P_0P0​ to rrr. If P0P_0P0​ lies on the line, the numerator is 000.

Definition 5.3 Pencils of lines in the module

The improper pencil (fascio improprio) is the set of all the lines parallel to a given line: y=mx+qy = mx + qy=mx+q with mmm fixed and qqq varying; the vertical lines form the pencil x=kx = kx=k, with kkk varying. The proper pencil (fascio proprio) with centre C=(xC,yC)C = (x_C, y_C)C=(xC​,yC​) is the set of all the lines through CCC: y−yC=m(x−xC)y - y_C = m(x - x_C)y−yC​=m(x−xC​) as mmm varies, plus the vertical line x=xCx = x_Cx=xC​. If two lines ax+by+c=0ax + by + c = 0ax+by+c=0 and a′x+b′y+c′=0a'x + b'y + c' = 0a′x+b′y+c′=0 meet at CCC, the proper pencil can also be written λ(ax+by+c)+μ(a′x+b′y+c′)=0\lambda(ax + by + c) + \mu(a'x + b'y + c') = 0λ(ax+by+c)+μ(a′x+b′y+c′)=0, with λ\lambdaλ (lambda) and μ\muμ (mu) real numbers that are not both zero.

5.2 Conic sections

Definition 5.4 Circle in the module

The circle (circonferenza) with centre CCC and radius r>0r > 0r>0 is the locus of the points PPP of the plane at distance rrr from CCC: d(P,C)=rd(P, C) = rd(P,C)=r. “Locus” means: the set of all and only the points with that property.

Rule 5.7 Equation of the circle in the module
(x−α)2+(y−β)2=r2(x - \alpha)^2 + (y - \beta)^2 = r^2(x−α)2+(y−β)2=r2

Expanding the squares you get the form x2+y2+ax+by+c=0x^2 + y^2 + ax + by + c = 0x2+y2+ax+by+c=0, from which

C=(−a2,−b2),r=a24+b24−cC = \left(-\frac{a}{2}, -\frac{b}{2}\right), \qquad r = \sqrt{\frac{a^2}{4} + \frac{b^2}{4} - c}C=(−2a​,−2b​),r=4a2​+4b2​−c​

The equation represents a real circle only if a24+b24−c≥0\frac{a^2}{4} + \frac{b^2}{4} - c \ge 04a2​+4b2​−c≥0, that is a2+b2−4c≥0a^2 + b^2 - 4c \ge 0a2+b2−4c≥0; if this quantity is 000, the “circle” reduces to the centre alone.

Rule 5.8 Position of a line relative to a circle in the module

Let ddd be the distance of the centre CCC from the line and rrr the radius:

  • d>rd > rd>r: non-intersecting line (retta esterna), no common point;
  • d=rd = rd=r: tangent line, exactly one common point;
  • d<rd < rd<r: secant line, two common points.

You get the same result by putting the line and the circle into a system: the second-degree equation you obtain has Δ<0\Delta < 0Δ<0, Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0 or Δ>0\Delta > 0Δ>0.

Rule 5.9 Properties of the pencil of circles in the module
  • The points common to C1C_1C1​ and C2C_2C2​ belong to all the circles of the pencil and to the radical axis.
  • The centres of all the circles of the pencil lie on the line of centres (asse centrale), the line through the centres of C1C_1C1​ and C2C_2C2​; the radical axis is perpendicular to the line of centres.
  • If C1C_1C1​ and C2C_2C2​ cut each other at two points, the radical axis is the line through those points; if they are tangent, it passes through the point of contact; if they have no common points, the radical axis does not meet any circle of the pencil.
  • Through every point of the plane passes one element of the pencil (a circle or the radical axis): the pencil “fills” the plane.
Definition 5.5 Parabola in the module

Given a point FFF, the focus, and a line fff that does not pass through FFF, the directrix, the parabola is the locus of the points PPP equidistant from the focus and from the directrix: d(P,F)=d(P,f)d(P, F) = d(P, f)d(P,F)=d(P,f). The point of the parabola closest to the focus and to the directrix is the vertex VVV; the line through FFF perpendicular to the directrix is the axis of symmetry.

Rule 5.10 Parabola with its vertex at the origin in the module
  • Focus (0,c)(0, c)(0,c) and directrix y=−cy = -cy=−c: the parabola is y=ax2y = ax^2y=ax2 with a=14ca = \frac{1}{4c}a=4c1​. Its axis is the yyy-axis; the focus is (0,14a)\left(0, \frac{1}{4a}\right)(0,4a1​) and the directrix y=−14ay = -\frac{1}{4a}y=−4a1​.
  • Focus (c,0)(c, 0)(c,0) and directrix x=−cx = -cx=−c: the parabola is x=ay2x = ay^2x=ay2, with the xxx-axis as its axis, focus (14a,0)\left(\frac{1}{4a}, 0\right)(4a1​,0) and directrix x=−14ax = -\frac{1}{4a}x=−4a1​.

In y=ax2y = ax^2y=ax2: if a>0a > 0a>0 the parabola is concave up (it opens upwards), if a<0a < 0a<0 it opens downwards; the larger ∣a∣|a|∣a∣, the narrower the parabola. In x=ay2x = ay^2x=ay2: it opens to the right if a>0a > 0a>0, to the left if a<0a < 0a<0.

Rule 5.11 Parabola with a vertical axis in the module

y=ax2+bx+cy = ax^2 + bx + cy=ax2+bx+c, with a≠0a \ne 0a=0 and Δ=b2−4ac\Delta = b^2 - 4acΔ=b2−4ac:

  • vertex V=(−b2a,−Δ4a)V = \left(-\frac{b}{2a}, -\frac{\Delta}{4a}\right)V=(−2ab​,−4aΔ​);
  • axis of symmetry x=−b2ax = -\frac{b}{2a}x=−2ab​;
  • focus F=(−b2a,1−Δ4a)F = \left(-\frac{b}{2a}, \frac{1 - \Delta}{4a}\right)F=(−2ab​,4a1−Δ​) and directrix y=−1+Δ4ay = -\frac{1 + \Delta}{4a}y=−4a1+Δ​;
  • it crosses the yyy-axis at (0,c)(0, c)(0,c) and the xxx-axis at the solutions of ax2+bx+c=0ax^2 + bx + c = 0ax2+bx+c=0: two points if Δ>0\Delta > 0Δ>0, only one (the vertex) if Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0, none if Δ<0\Delta < 0Δ<0.

aaa determines which way the parabola opens and how wide it is; bbb and ccc move the parabola.

Definition 5.6 Ellipse in the module

Given two points FFF and F′F'F′, the foci, the ellipse is the locus of the points PPP for which the sum of the distances from the foci is constant: d(P,F)+d(P,F′)=2ad(P, F) + d(P, F') = 2ad(P,F)+d(P,F′)=2a, with 2a>d(F,F′)2a > d(F, F')2a>d(F,F′).

Rule 5.12 Standard equation of the ellipse in the module

With the foci F=(c,0)F = (c, 0)F=(c,0) and F′=(−c,0)F' = (-c, 0)F′=(−c,0) on the xxx-axis and the centre at the origin:

x2a2+y2b2=1,b2=a2−c2(a>b)\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1, \qquad b^2 = a^2 - c^2 \quad (a > b)a2x2​+b2y2​=1,b2=a2−c2(a>b)
  • vertices A=(a,0)A = (a, 0)A=(a,0), A′=(−a,0)A' = (-a, 0)A′=(−a,0), B=(0,b)B = (0, b)B=(0,b), B′=(0,−b)B' = (0, -b)B′=(0,−b); centre OOO;
  • symmetric with respect to both axes and to the origin; contained in the rectangle −a≤x≤a-a \le x \le a−a≤x≤a, −b≤y≤b-b \le y \le b−b≤y≤b;
  • eccentricity e=cae = \frac{c}{a}e=ac​, with 0≤e<10 \le e < 10≤e<1: the closer it is to 000, the “rounder” the ellipse. If a=ba = ba=b then c=0c = 0c=0 and the ellipse is a circle.

If in the equation b>ab > ab>a, the foci lie on the yyy-axis: (0,±c)(0, \pm c)(0,±c) with c2=b2−a2c^2 = b^2 - a^2c2=b2−a2, and the eccentricity is cb\frac{c}{b}bc​ (always the ratio between ccc and the semi-major axis).

Definition 5.7 Hyperbola in the module

Given the foci FFF and F′F'F′, the hyperbola is the locus of the points PPP for which the difference of the distances from the foci, in absolute value, is constant: ∣d(P,F)−d(P,F′)∣=2a|d(P, F) - d(P, F')| = 2a∣d(P,F)−d(P,F′)∣=2a, with 2a<d(F,F′)2a < d(F, F')2a<d(F,F′).

Rule 5.13 Standard equation of the hyperbola in the module

With the foci F=(c,0)F = (c, 0)F=(c,0) and F′=(−c,0)F' = (-c, 0)F′=(−c,0):

x2a2−y2b2=1,b2=c2−a2(c2=a2+b2)\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1, \qquad b^2 = c^2 - a^2 \quad (c^2 = a^2 + b^2)a2x2​−b2y2​=1,b2=c2−a2(c2=a2+b2)
  • vertices A=(a,0)A = (a, 0)A=(a,0) and A′=(−a,0)A' = (-a, 0)A′=(−a,0), where the hyperbola is tangent to the lines x=±ax = \pm ax=±a; no point on the yyy-axis and no point with −a<x<a-a < x < a−a<x<a, so the curve is made up of two branches;
  • symmetric with respect to both axes and to the origin;
  • asymptotes y=±baxy = \pm\frac{b}{a}xy=±ab​x: lines through the origin that the branches get closer and closer to without ever touching them; they are the diagonals of the rectangle with vertices (±a,±b)(\pm a, \pm b)(±a,±b);
  • eccentricity e=ca>1e = \frac{c}{a} > 1e=ac​>1.

The equation x2a2−y2b2=−1\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = -1a2x2​−b2y2​=−1 is a hyperbola with vertices (0,±b)(0, \pm b)(0,±b) and foci (0,±c)(0, \pm c)(0,±c) on the yyy-axis; the asymptotes are still y=±baxy = \pm\frac{b}{a}xy=±ab​x and again c2=a2+b2c^2 = a^2 + b^2c2=a2+b2.

Rule 5.14 Rectangular hyperbola in the module

If a=ba = ba=b the hyperbola is called rectangular (iperbole equilatera): x2−y2=a2x^2 - y^2 = a^2x2−y2=a2. The asymptotes are the bisectors y=xy = xy=x and y=−xy = -xy=−x, perpendicular to each other; the foci are (±a2,0)(\pm a\sqrt2, 0)(±a2​,0) and the eccentricity is 2\sqrt22​. The equation x2−y2=0x^2 - y^2 = 0x2−y2=0, that is (x−y)(x+y)=0(x - y)(x + y) = 0(x−y)(x+y)=0, represents the two bisectors: it is a degenerate hyperbola.

Rule 5.15 Rectangular hyperbola referred to its asymptotes in the module

If the two asymptotes are taken as the Cartesian axes, the rectangular hyperbola has equation

xy=k(k≠0)xy = k \qquad (k \ne 0)xy=k(k=0)

The asymptotes are the xxx- and yyy-axes. If k>0k > 0k>0 the branches lie in quadrants I and III and the vertices are on the bisector y=xy = xy=x, at (k,k)(\sqrt{k}, \sqrt{k})(k​,k​) and (−k,−k)(-\sqrt{k}, -\sqrt{k})(−k​,−k​); the foci lie on the same bisector, at (2k,2k)(\sqrt{2k}, \sqrt{2k})(2k​,2k​) and (−2k,−2k)(-\sqrt{2k}, -\sqrt{2k})(−2k​,−2k​); if k<0k < 0k<0 the branches lie in quadrants II and IV and the vertices are on the bisector y=−xy = -xy=−x. It is the graph of y=kxy = \frac{k}{x}y=xk​, inverse proportionality.

Module 6. Real functions of a real variable

Notes for module 6, with explanations, examples and exercises.

6.1 Definition of a function and main features

Definition 6.1 Function in the module

A function fff from a set AAA to a set BBB is a rule that assigns to every element xxx of AAA one and only one element of BBB, denoted by f(x)f(x)f(x). You write

f:A→B,x↦f(x)f: A \to B, \qquad x \mapsto f(x)f:A→B,x↦f(x)

and read “fff from AAA to BBB, which maps xxx to f(x)f(x)f(x)”. Here AAA and BBB are subsets of R\RR, the set of real numbers: we speak of real functions of a real variable. You often write y=f(x)y = f(x)y=f(x).

Definition 6.2 Graph in the module

The graph of fff is the set of the points (x,f(x))(x, f(x))(x,f(x)) of the plane, with xxx in the domain. A curve is the graph of a function if and only if every vertical line meets it in at most one point: two points on the same vertical line would mean two values for the same xxx.

Definition 6.3 Injective, surjective, bijective in the module
  • fff is injective if distinct elements of the domain have distinct images: x1≠x2⇒f(x1)≠f(x2)x_1 \ne x_2 \Rightarrow f(x_1) \ne f(x_2)x1​=x2​⇒f(x1​)=f(x2​) (the arrow ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ reads “implies”). Equivalently: f(x1)=f(x2)⇒x1=x2f(x_1) = f(x_2) \Rightarrow x_1 = x_2f(x1​)=f(x2​)⇒x1​=x2​. An injective function never takes the same value twice.
  • f:A→Bf: A \to Bf:A→B is surjective if every element of the codomain is the image of at least one element of the domain: for every y∈By \in By∈B there exists x∈Ax \in Ax∈A with f(x)=yf(x) = yf(x)=y (the symbol ∈\in∈ reads “belongs to”). In other words f(A)=Bf(A) = Bf(A)=B.
  • fff is bijective (in Italian biiettiva or biunivoca) if it is both injective and surjective: there is a one-to-one correspondence between domain and codomain.
Definition 6.4 Restriction in the module

If D⊆AD \subseteq AD⊆A (DDD is contained in AAA), the restriction of fff to DDD is the function f∣D:D→Bf|_D: D \to Bf∣D​:D→B that acts like fff but only on the points of DDD: f∣D(x)=f(x)f|_D(x) = f(x)f∣D​(x)=f(x) for every x∈Dx \in Dx∈D. The domain is restricted; the codomain stays the same.

Definition 6.5 Inverse function in the module

If f:A→Bf: A \to Bf:A→B is bijective, its inverse f−1:B→Af^{-1}: B \to Af−1:B→A (read “fff inverse” or “fff to the minus one”) assigns to every y∈By \in By∈B the unique x∈Ax \in Ax∈A such that f(x)=yf(x) = yf(x)=y. So f−1(f(x))=xf^{-1}(f(x)) = xf−1(f(x))=x and f(f−1(y))=yf(f^{-1}(y)) = yf(f−1(y))=y: the dependent variable of fff becomes the independent variable of f−1f^{-1}f−1. A function is invertible if and only if it is bijective, and the domain of f−1f^{-1}f−1 is the range of fff. The graph of f−1f^{-1}f−1 is symmetric to that of fff with respect to the bisector y=xy = xy=x.

Definition 6.6 Composite function in the module

Given f:A→Bf: A \to Bf:A→B and g:B→Cg: B \to Cg:B→C, the composite g∘fg \circ fg∘f (read “ggg composed with fff”) is the function from AAA to CCC defined by

(g∘f)(x)=g(f(x))(g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x))(g∘f)(x)=g(f(x))

You apply fff first (the inner function) and then ggg (the outer function). For this to be possible, the range of fff must be contained in the domain of ggg; if it is not, you restrict the domain of fff.

Definition 6.7 Even and odd in the module

The domain must be symmetric with respect to 000: if it contains xxx, it also contains −x-x−x.

  • fff is even if f(−x)=f(x)f(-x) = f(x)f(−x)=f(x) for every xxx in the domain: the graph is symmetric with respect to the yyy-axis.
  • fff is odd if f(−x)=−f(x)f(-x) = -f(x)f(−x)=−f(x) for every xxx in the domain: the graph is symmetric with respect to the origin.
Definition 6.8 Periodic function in the module

fff is periodic with period T>0T > 0T>0 if f(x+T)=f(x)f(x + T) = f(x)f(x+T)=f(x) for every xxx in the domain, and TTT is the smallest positive number with this property. The graph repeats identically every TTT: it is enough to study it on an interval of length TTT.

Definition 6.9 Monotonicity on an interval III of the domain in the module

For every x1,x2∈Ix_1, x_2 \in Ix1​,x2​∈I with x1<x2x_1 < x_2x1​<x2​:

  • fff is increasing on III if f(x1)<f(x2)f(x_1) < f(x_2)f(x1​)<f(x2​): the graph, traced from left to right, goes up;
  • fff is decreasing on III if f(x1)>f(x2)f(x_1) > f(x_2)f(x1​)>f(x2​): the graph goes down;
  • fff is non-decreasing on III if f(x1)≤f(x2)f(x_1) \le f(x_2)f(x1​)≤f(x2​), non-increasing if f(x1)≥f(x2)f(x_1) \ge f(x_2)f(x1​)≥f(x2​): horizontal pieces are allowed.

A function that has one of these properties on III is called monotonic on III. Some books call “strictly increasing” what is called increasing here, and “increasing” what is called non-decreasing here.

Definition 6.10 Bounded function in the module
  • fff is bounded above if there is a number KKK such that f(x)≤Kf(x) \le Kf(x)≤K for every xxx in the domain;
  • fff is bounded below if there is a number KKK such that f(x)≥Kf(x) \ge Kf(x)≥K for every xxx in the domain;
  • fff is bounded if it is both bounded above and bounded below: its graph lies entirely within a horizontal strip of the plane.
Rule 6.1 Translating the graph of fff (with c>0c > 0c>0) in the module
  • y=f(x−c)y = f(x - c)y=f(x−c): the graph of fff shifted to the right by ccc;
  • y=f(x+c)y = f(x + c)y=f(x+c): shifted to the left by ccc;
  • y=f(x)+cy = f(x) + cy=f(x)+c: shifted up by ccc;
  • y=f(x)−cy = f(x) - cy=f(x)−c: shifted down by ccc.

If the constant is inside the argument, the translation is horizontal and goes “against” the sign; if it is outside, it is vertical and follows the sign. Together: y=f(x−h)+ky = f(x - h) + ky=f(x−h)+k is the graph of fff shifted by hhh horizontally and by kkk vertically.

6.2 Examples of useful functions

Definition 6.11 Constant function in the module

f:R→Rf: \R \to \Rf:R→R, f(x)=kf(x) = kf(x)=k, with kkk a fixed real number: all the elements of the domain have the same image kkk. The graph is the horizontal line y=ky = ky=k.

Definition 6.12 Absolute value in the module
f(x)=∣x∣={xif x≥0−xif x<0f(x) = |x| = \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0 \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0 \end{cases}f(x)=∣x∣={x−x​if x≥0if x<0​

The graph is a “V” with its vertex at the origin, made up of the bisector y=xy = xy=x for x≥0x \ge 0x≥0 and of y=−xy = -xy=−x for x<0x < 0x<0. The function is even, has range [0,+∞)[0, +\infty)[0,+∞), is decreasing on (−∞,0](-\infty, 0](−∞,0] and increasing on [0,+∞)[0, +\infty)[0,+∞).

Definition 6.13 Linear function in the module

f:R→Rf: \R \to \Rf:R→R, f(x)=mx+qf(x) = mx + qf(x)=mx+q, with mmm and qqq real: the graph is the line with slope mmm and yyy-intercept qqq. If q=0q = 0q=0 it becomes y=mxy = mxy=mx and the line passes through the origin.

Definition 6.14 Direct proportionality in the module

Two quantities xxx and yyy are directly proportional if y=kxy = kxy=kx, with k≠0k \ne 0k=0 constant, that is if the ratio yx\frac{y}{x}xy​ is constant (for x≠0x \ne 0x=0). If xxx doubles, yyy doubles; if xxx triples, yyy triples. The number kkk is the constant of proportionality and the graph is a line through the origin.

Definition 6.15 Inverse proportionality in the module

Two quantities are inversely proportional if y=kxy = \frac{k}{x}y=xk​, with k≠0k \ne 0k=0 constant, that is if the product xy=kxy = kxy=k is constant. If xxx doubles, yyy halves. The simplest case is

f(x)=1x,x≠0f(x) = \frac{1}{x}, \qquad x \ne 0f(x)=x1​,x=0

whose graph is the rectangular hyperbola referred to its asymptotes, xy=1xy = 1xy=1: the asymptotes are the Cartesian axes.

Definition 7.1 Exponential function in the module

Given a number aaa with a>0a > 0a>0 and a≠1a \neq 1a=1, the exponential function with base aaa is the function f(x)=axf(x) = a^xf(x)=ax, which assigns to every real number xxx the number axa^xax.

Rule 7.2 Features of y=axy = a^xy=ax in the module
  • Domain: all of R\RR, the set of real numbers: every xxx is allowed.
  • Sign: ax>0a^x > 0ax>0 always; the range (image) is the interval (0,+∞)(0, +\infty)(0,+∞), where the symbol ∞\infty∞ reads “infinity”.
  • Key points: the graph always passes through (0,1)(0, 1)(0,1), because a0=1a^0 = 1a0=1, and through (1,a)(1, a)(1,a), because a1=aa^1 = aa1=a.
  • Monotonicity: if a>1a > 1a>1 the function is increasing, if 0<a<10 < a < 10<a<1 it is decreasing. In both cases it is monotonic, so au=ava^u = a^vau=av only when u=vu = vu=v.
  • Asymptote: the graph approaches the xxx-axis without ever touching it (the xxx-axis is a horizontal asymptote): towards the left if a>1a > 1a>1, towards the right if 0<a<10 < a < 10<a<1.
Rule 7.3 Comparing two powers with the same base in the module
  • If a>1a > 1a>1: au<ava^u < a^vau<av exactly when u<vu < vu<v (the order of the exponents is preserved).
  • If 0<a<10 < a < 10<a<1: au<ava^u < a^vau<av exactly when u>vu > vu>v (the order is reversed).

In symbols, for a>1a > 1a>1 you write au<av  ⟺  u<va^u < a^v \iff u < vau<av⟺u<v, where   ⟺  \iff⟺ reads “if and only if”.

Definition 7.2 Logarithm in the module

Let a>0a > 0a>0 with a≠1a \neq 1a=1, and b>0b > 0b>0. The logarithm of bbb to base aaa, written log⁡ab\log_a bloga​b, is the exponent to which you must raise aaa to obtain bbb:

log⁡ab=y  ⟺  ay=b\log_a b = y \iff a^y = bloga​b=y⟺ay=b

The number aaa is the base, the number bbb is the argument of the logarithm.

Rule 7.4 Four equalities to know by heart in the module

For every allowed base aaa:

  • log⁡a1=0\log_a 1 = 0loga​1=0, because a0=1a^0 = 1a0=1;
  • log⁡aa=1\log_a a = 1loga​a=1, because a1=aa^1 = aa1=a;
  • log⁡aax=x\log_a a^x = xloga​ax=x for every real xxx: the logarithm “undoes” the power;
  • alog⁡ax=xa^{\log_a x} = xaloga​x=x for every x>0x > 0x>0: the power “undoes” the logarithm.

Definition 7.3 Logarithmic function in the module

Given a>0a > 0a>0 with a≠1a \neq 1a=1, the logarithmic function with base aaa is the function f(x)=log⁡axf(x) = \log_a xf(x)=loga​x, defined for x>0x > 0x>0.

Rule 7.6 Features of y=log⁡axy = \log_a xy=loga​x in the module
  • Domain: (0,+∞)(0, +\infty)(0,+∞): only positive arguments.
  • Range: all of R\RR.
  • Key points: the graph passes through (1,0)(1, 0)(1,0), because log⁡a1=0\log_a 1 = 0loga​1=0, and through (a,1)(a, 1)(a,1).
  • Monotonicity: increasing if a>1a > 1a>1, decreasing if 0<a<10 < a < 10<a<1.
  • Asymptote: the yyy-axis is a vertical asymptote: near x=0x = 0x=0 the graph goes down towards −∞-\infty−∞ if a>1a > 1a>1 and up towards +∞+\infty+∞ if 0<a<10 < a < 10<a<1.
  • Sign: if a>1a > 1a>1, log⁡ax\log_a xloga​x is negative for 0<x<10 < x < 10<x<1 and positive for x>1x > 1x>1; if 0<a<10 < a < 10<a<1 the opposite happens.
Rule 7.7 Inverse functions in the module

With the same base aaa:

log⁡a(ax)=x  for every x∈R,alog⁡ax=x  for every x>0\log_a\left(a^x\right) = x \ \text{ for every } x \in \R, \qquad a^{\log_a x} = x \ \text{ for every } x > 0loga​(ax)=x  for every x∈R,aloga​x=x  for every x>0

(∈\in∈ reads “belongs to”). Each function undoes the other: y=axy = a^xy=ax and y=log⁡axy = \log_a xy=loga​x are inverse functions. Their graphs are symmetric with respect to the line y=xy = xy=x, the bisector of the first and third quadrants: if the point (p,q)(p, q)(p,q) lies on the graph of the exponential, the point (q,p)(q, p)(q,p) lies on the graph of the logarithm.

7.2 Exponential and logarithmic equations and inequalities

Rule 7.8 The direction depends on the base in the module
  • If a>1a > 1a>1: af(x)>ag(x)  ⟺  f(x)>g(x)a^{f(x)} > a^{g(x)} \iff f(x) > g(x)af(x)>ag(x)⟺f(x)>g(x) (the direction stays the same).
  • If 0<a<10 < a < 10<a<1: af(x)>ag(x)  ⟺  f(x)<g(x)a^{f(x)} > a^{g(x)} \iff f(x) < g(x)af(x)>ag(x)⟺f(x)<g(x) (the direction is reversed).

The same holds with <<<, ≥\geq≥, ≤\leq≤. The reason is monotonicity: with a base greater than 1 the exponential increases, with a base between 0 and 1 it decreases.

With f(x)>0f(x) > 0f(x)>0 and g(x)>0g(x) > 0g(x)>0:

  • if 0<a<10 < a < 10<a<1: log⁡af(x)>log⁡ag(x)  ⟺  f(x)<g(x)\log_a f(x) > \log_a g(x) \iff f(x) < g(x)loga​f(x)>loga​g(x)⟺f(x)<g(x) (the direction is reversed).

Module 8. Trigonometry

Introduction: unit circle and angles

Definition 8.1 Unit circle in the module

The unit circle (circonferenza goniometrica) is the circle in the Cartesian plane with centre at the origin OOO and radius 1. Its equation is x2+y2=1x^2 + y^2 = 1x2+y2=1.

Definition 8.2 Degree and radian in the module
  • The degree (1∘1^\circ1∘) is the angle corresponding to 1360\frac{1}{360}3601​ of the full angle.
  • The radian is the central angle that, on any circle, subtends an arc as long as the radius.
Rule 8.1 Converting between degrees and radians in the module

If α\alphaα is the measure in degrees and xxx the measure in radians, the proportion α:360=x:2π\alpha : 360 = x : 2\piα:360=x:2π holds, from which

x=α⋅π180α=x⋅180πx = \alpha \cdot \frac{\pi}{180} \qquad\qquad \alpha = x \cdot \frac{180}{\pi}x=α⋅180π​α=x⋅π180​

So P=(cos⁡x,sin⁡x)P = (\cos x, \sin x)P=(cosx,sinx).

For every angle xxx:

Rule 8.13 Edge cases in the module
  • sin⁡x>c\sin x > csinx>c with c<−1c < -1c<−1: true for every xxx. With c≥1c \geq 1c≥1: no solutions.
  • sin⁡x≥1\sin x \geq 1sinx≥1: the sine never exceeds 1, so it is true only when sin⁡x=1\sin x = 1sinx=1, that is for x=π2+2kπx = \frac{\pi}{2} + 2k\pix=2π​+2kπ.
  • sin⁡x>−1\sin x > -1sinx>−1: true for every xxx except x=3π2+2kπx = \frac{3\pi}{2} + 2k\pix=23π​+2kπ.
  • cos⁡x<1\cos x < 1cosx<1: true for every xxx except x=2kπx = 2k\pix=2kπ. cos⁡x≤1\cos x \leq 1cosx≤1: true for every xxx.
  • sin⁡x<2\sin x < 2sinx<2: true for every xxx. cos⁡x>32\cos x > \frac32cosx>23​: no solutions.
Rule 8.14 Right-angled triangle (right angle at CCC, hypotenuse ccc) in the module
  • a=csin⁡α=ccos⁡βa = c\sin\alpha = c\cos\betaa=csinα=ccosβ and b=csin⁡β=ccos⁡αb = c\sin\beta = c\cos\alphab=csinβ=ccosα: a leg is the hypotenuse times the sine of the opposite angle, or times the cosine of the adjacent acute angle.
  • a=btan⁡α=bcotan⁡βa = b\tan\alpha = b\operatorname{cotan}\betaa=btanα=bcotanβ and b=atan⁡β=acotan⁡αb = a\tan\beta = a\operatorname{cotan}\alphab=atanβ=acotanα: a leg is the other leg times the tangent of the angle opposite the first leg, or times the cotangent of the angle adjacent to the first leg.
  • α+β=90∘\alpha + \beta = 90^\circα+β=90∘.

In words: sin⁡α=opposite leghypotenuse\sin\alpha = \dfrac{\text{opposite leg}}{\text{hypotenuse}}sinα=hypotenuseopposite leg​, cos⁡α=adjacent leghypotenuse\cos\alpha = \dfrac{\text{adjacent leg}}{\text{hypotenuse}}cosα=hypotenuseadjacent leg​, tan⁡α=opposite legadjacent leg\tan\alpha = \dfrac{\text{opposite leg}}{\text{adjacent leg}}tanα=adjacent legopposite leg​.

Rule 8.15 Any triangle in the module

Law of cosines (also called Carnot's theorem): the square of a side is the sum of the squares of the other two, minus twice their product times the cosine of the angle between them.

a2=b2+c2−2bccos⁡αb2=a2+c2−2accos⁡βc2=a2+b2−2abcos⁡γa^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos\alpha \qquad b^2 = a^2 + c^2 - 2ac\cos\beta \qquad c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos\gammaa2=b2+c2−2bccosαb2=a2+c2−2accosβc2=a2+b2−2abcosγ

With a right angle the cosine is 0 and you get back Pythagoras' theorem.

Law of sines: the sides are proportional to the sines of the opposite angles.

asin⁡α=bsin⁡β=csin⁡γ\frac{a}{\sin\alpha} = \frac{b}{\sin\beta} = \frac{c}{\sin\gamma}sinαa​=sinβb​=sinγc​

The law of cosines is used when you know two sides and the angle between them (to find the third side) or three sides (to find an angle). The law of sines is used when you know two angles and a side. Also remember that α+β+γ=180∘\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 180^\circα+β+γ=180∘.
